newsitem.title: UK: UK ministers excluded rail profits clawback - OPRAF.
newsitem.headline: UK ministers excluded rail profits clawback - OPRAF.

text.p: The director of Britain's Office of Passenger Rail Franchising said on Monday that ministers had instructed him not to include a provision for the clawback of high profits in franchises offered to rail service operators.
Roger Salmon, giving evidence to Parliament's Public Accounts Committee, said the government had been worried that clawback provisions would reduce companies' incentives to increase efficiency.
The committee was questioning Salmon over the awarding of the first three franchises to run trains over track previously operated by state-owned British Rail in December last year.

Committee chairman Robert Sheldon put it to him that since the 30 bidders for the franchises had no previous experience of running passenger services, they might have made bids which would enable them to make artificially high profits.
He suggested there should therefore have been a provision for clawback.
Salmon replied: "I discussed the matter at length with ministers who instructed me that I should not have a provision for clawback and therefore I did not."
"Ministers' reasons related to two specific things," he added.

"One -- without clawback you can expect at least to some degree to get a better base bid, and secondly, if you have clawback, at the margin you reduce the incentive effect on bidders to perform and they wanted to have the maximum possible incentive."

The first three franchises were South West Trains, which went to Stagecoach Holdings Plc, Great Western Trains, awarded to Great Western Holdings and LTS Rail, which was finally awarded to Prism Rail Plc.
